The Egyptians, Babylonians and Chinese from long ago knew of a special connection between the lengths of the sides of triangles and they used this relationship. However, the first person to define this relationship was Pythagoras, a Greek mathematician and philosopher (582 BC–500 BC). He established a school of philosophy in Italy where he and his followers expressed views that were considered strange at the time (such as that the earth rotates around its own axis and that the planets revolve around the sun). As a result of these theories, Pythagoras was forced to flee to Egypt.
In any right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares on the adjacent sides.
• In a right-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is equal to the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides (the sides adjacent to the right angle).
• In an acute-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is smaller than the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides.
• In an obtuse-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is larger than the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides.
• Squares are the easiest similar shapes to construct on the sides of a triangle.
• It is the easiest to calculate the area of squares.

Identify the cardinal points on a compass
The focus in this section is on finding compass directions.

In the Starter activity, you probably used words such as north, south, east and west to describe the direction from one place to another. These four words represent the cardinal (main) points N, S, E and W on a magnetic compass.

There is a big difference between the directions shown by the four cardinal points on a compass and so four points halfway between the cardinal points are used: northeast (NE), northwest (NW), southeast (SE) and southwest (SW). These four points and the four cardinal points make it possible to describe the direction of one place or object from another in different ways.

• · Description by referring to direction:
    • » Our classroom faces east.
    • » My bedroom has a north-facing window.
    • » The clinic is about 6 km southwest of our house.

• · Description by referring to places in general:
    • » Our teacher comes from the northern part of the country.
    • » The tourist capital is in the southern part of the country.
    • » Most of our mining industries are in the northwestern part of the country.

• · Description by referring to particular places:
    • » Zambia is in southern central Africa and Japan in southeastern Asia.
    • » Spain lies in the southwestern part of Europe.
    • » The 2014 FIFA World Cup was held in the easterly part of South America.

• Description by referring to movement:
    • » A learner walked 10 km to school in an easterly direction from home.
    • » The cyclist cycled southwards and the bus travelled westwards.
    • » The aeroplane flies in a northeasterly direction.

People invest money so that its value can increase. There are different ways to invest money, such as depositing money in a savings account at a bank and buying bonds or shares (stocks). An investment can appreciate (grow or increase) over time. This means that it grows and its value increases. In the same way, its value can also depreciate.
This means that over time, the value becomes lower than the initial value.

An investment can be an asset such as a stock, a bond, currency (money) or real estate (property such as a house or an office block). It can also refer to objects a company owns such as a fleet of cars and a piece of machinery.
We invest money so that it will grow.

This person or company invests (loans) their money (the principal amount) to the borrower in the form of bonds. What is the order of a matrix?

The number of rows and columns a matrix contains is called its order. The order of a matrix determines the size and shape of the matrix. A matrix of order 3 by 2 has 3 rows and 2 columns, and a matrix of order 2 by 3 has 2 rows and 3 columns. Look at the examples:
• \frac{3}{2} has 2 rows and 1 column, therefore it is a 2 by 1 (2 × 1) matrix
• \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} has 2 rows and 2 columns, therefore it is a 2 by 2 (2 × 2) matrix
• \frac{2}{8} has 2 rows and 3 columns, therefore it is a 2 by 3 (2 × 3) matrix.
We always write the number of rows first when we give the order of a matrix.

Probability is the branch of mathematics that makes it possible for us to predict the likelihood that something (an event) will happen (occur). It helps us make decisions about choices in areas such as business, weather forecasts, health, education, gambling (betting) and engineering. People use probability practically in every field. This is why it is important.
In order to study probability in a precise and clear way, we need to define terminology and notations:
trial: an action that can have more than one result
• tossing a coin: heads (H) or tails (T)
• tossing a coin and throwing a dice (H (heads) and T (tails)): H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 or T6
• tossing a coin: heads (H) or tails (T)
• tossing a coin and throwing a dice: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 or T6
event: something that can or cannot occur (happen) when a trial is conducted examples:
• throwing a dice and scoring less than 7: a certain event something that will occur (all the possible outcomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) are smaller than 7)
• throwing a dice and scoring 7: an impossible event something that cannot occur (none of the possible outcomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) is 7)
• throwing a dice and scoring an even number: a possible event something that can occur (three of the possible outcomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6) are even numbers)
• · tossing a coin three times: experiment consists of three trials
• · throwing a dice ten times: experiment consists of ten trials
• · tossing a coin and throwing a dice together five times: experiment consists of five trials
• throwing a dice and scoring a number smaller than 7: all possible outcomes are smaller than 7
• throwing two dice and scoring a whole number in total: all possible outcomes from 2 to 12 are whole numbers
• · taking a red pen from a bag: certain if the bag contains only red pens
• throwing a dice and scoring 7: a dice does not include the number 7
• throwing two dice and scoring a total of 1: the smallest possible outcome is 2
• · taking a red pen from a bag: impossible if there are no red pens in the bag
equally likely events: same (equal) chance of occurring examples:
• When we toss a fair coin, the event of scoring heads is as equally likely to occur as the event of scoring tails.
• When we throw a fair dice, the event of scoring 1 is as equally likely to occur as any of the events of scoring 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.

random occurrence of an event: there is no certain way of predicting when and where the event will occur examples:
• · If we toss a fair coin, we cannot predict whether heads or tails will occur.

sample space (S) of a random trial or experiment: a set of all the possible outcomes of the particular trial or experiment examples:

As you have learnt, you can find experimental probability by conducting an experiment and observing the outcomes. However, when identical experiments are conducted, their outcomes may differ. We can overcome this obvious disadvantage of experimental probability by assigning theoretical probabilities to the events in a sample space. These probabilities are based on the results of an ideal experiment.
We can investigate this by finding the theoretical probability of obtaining tails (T) when you toss a coin once.

There are two equally likely ways a coin can land if you toss it, and there is only one way a coin can land with tails facing up. The probability that you will get tails if you toss a coin is \frac{1}{2}.

There is one favourable outcome for the event: {T}. The numerator shows the number of favourable outcomes. There are two possible outcomes for this trial: {H, T}. The denominator shows the number of possible outcomes.
We can deduce that we can calculate theoretical probability by dividing the number of favourable outcomes of an event by the number of possible outcomes of the trial or experiment.
The possible outcomes of a trial or experiment are all the different results that can occur. We call the set that contains these outcomes the sample space (S) of the trial. Examples:
• Sample space of the trial {tossing a coin}: S = {H, T}

We see great athletes at the Olympics and at other races. They make sprinting and jumping look easy. The fact is that they practise every day - they do not stand around and watch other athletes practise. They practise all the important aspects: starting a race, building up to the right speed, maintaining their speed, and not allowing spectators or other athletes to distract them. They practise in spite of bad weather, tiredness and distractions.

To be successful in Mathematics, you have to practise your skills. You cannot just watch your teacher explain something, think that you understand, close your books and walk away. You need to be involved. Ask questions when you do not understand something. Listen to explanations. Apply new information. Use the answers that are given in this Learner's Book to check whether you are on track or whether you need to ask for help. If you choose to do these things, your skills will improve. Every day in class can make a difference if you decide that improving your skills in Mathematics is important.

In a football match, players have to handle each situation that arises. They need to read the game and react appropriately. In a test or an exam, you need to read questions very carefully and make sure you understand what to do before you start answering a question. Reread questions if necessary. If you do not know how to answer a question, move to the next question and return to questions you have skipped if you have time later.

• Do you have to show your working? Marks are mostly allocated for showing calculations and not only for the answers.
